# Variable leases under ASC 842: ﬁrst evidence on properties and consequences

Jonas Heese1 · Albert Shin1 · Charles C.Y. Wang1

Extended author information available on the last page of the article

## 123

Accepted: 3 June 2025 © The Author(s) 2025

Abstract The new lease standard (ASC 842) allows ﬁrms to keep variable leases off balance sheet, in part based on the assumption that future expenses are difﬁcult to estimate reliably. We show that variable lease expenses are both prevalent and substantial, exhibiting persistence and predictability comparable to operating lease expenses while showing limited sensitivity to revenue changes. These patterns are consistent with variable lease payments being based on stable drivers. Following ASC 842 adoption, ﬁrms report lower minimum operating lease commitments and higher variable lease expenses, suggesting a substitution from operating to variable leases. Neither equity betas nor credit ratings reﬂect potential variable lease liabilities. Conservative estimates show that recognition of variable lease liabilities would increase debt by 7.1% on average. Our ﬁndings provide evidence on the properties of variable leases and the potential implications of keeping them off balance sheet.

Keywords ASC 842 · Lease Accounting · Reclassiﬁcation · Variable Leases · Off-balance-sheet liabilities

## 1 Introduction

Investors and other stakeholders have long criticized the inconsistent accounting treatment of ﬁnance and operating leases, with only ﬁnance leases being historically recognized on the balance sheet. The Securities and Exchange Commission (2005) argued that inconsistent lease treatment incentivized companies to strategically structure lease arrangements “to meet various accounting, tax, and other goals.” The new lease accounting standard ASU 2016-02, Lease (Topic 842), codiﬁed as ASC 842, aims to eliminate these differences by requiring balance-sheet recognition for both ﬁnance and operating leases. However, the Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) made an exception for leases with variable payments, which can remain off balance sheet—a provision affecting a substantial portion of total lease costs in some industries.1 The FASB (2016) attributed this decision in part to feedback from companies about the difﬁculty of reliably estimating variable lease payments, which could ﬂuctuate with the economic activity of the leased asset.2 This study performs several interrelated analyses to examine the properties of variable leases and the consequences of keeping variable lease costs off balance sheet. In its 2010 exposure draft of the new lease standard, the FASB initially proposed recognizing variable leases on the balance sheet, arguing that “such contingent rentals meet the deﬁnition of a liability” because lessor and lessee typically have “some level of understanding about the likely amount of payments” (p. 105, IASB/FASB (2010)). The board further reasoned: “The liability to pay contingent rentals and the right to receive lease payments exist at the date of inception of the lease. Such contingent rentals meet the deﬁnition of a liability for the lessee and an asset for the lessor. It is only the amount to be paid that is uncertain” (Section BC123, IASB/FASB (2010)). Companies challenged this position, arguing that reliably estimating variable lease liabilities is difﬁcult because payments are linked to asset usage or revenue generation manyyears intothefuture(FASB2016). For example, airlines’ leaseexpenses for gates and ticket counters typically depend on passenger trafﬁc, while retailers’ and banks’ lease expenses for stores and branches often depend on customer trafﬁc or revenues generated at each location (Eaglesham 2019; FASB 2016).3 The FASB ultimately allowed variable leases to remain off balance sheet under the new standard.4

The differential treatment of variable leases thus rests on the assumption that they exhibit properties unlike operating and ﬁnance leases—speciﬁcally, that variable lease payments are less persistent, less predictable, and more variable. Our ﬁrst set of analyses tests these assumptions using operating, ﬁnance, and variable lease expenses disclosed in ﬁrms’ footnotes, as required under ASC 842. However, our analysis is primarily based on comparing variable and operating lease expenses. Pragmatically, operating leases are far more common than ﬁnance leases, and thus this reference point allows us to preserve the largest sample size. Moreover, variable lease costs were typically a subcomponent of operating lease costs, representing an addition to the base operating lease payments; both were reported as rental or operating lease expenses on the income statement. Our sample includes U.S. public ﬁrms that belonged to the Russell 3000 index at any time between 2015 and 2021. Our descriptive statistics reveal that variable leases are common and economically signiﬁcant. More than 40% of the ﬁrms in our sample report variable lease expenses, and that number reaches 51% in 2022. Moreover, these expenses represent more than 25% of operating lease expenses for the average ﬁrm that reports both. We then document three properties of variable leases. First, variable lease expenses exhibit higher persistence than operating and ﬁnance lease expenses. Speciﬁcally, in two cross-sectional regression speciﬁcations, we obtain persistence parameters of 0.96 and 0.92 for variable lease expenses, similar to the estimates for operating (0.97 and 0.92) and ﬁnance lease (0.98 and 0.95) expenses. Second, variable lease expenses are at least as predictable as operating lease expenses. Using random walk forecasts for each of the three types of lease expenses, we ﬁnd that mean squared prediction errors for variable lease expense forecasts are signiﬁcantly lower (higher) than those for operating lease (ﬁnance lease) expense forecasts. Third, while variable leases respond more to changes in economic conditions than the other lease types, their revenue elasticity is economically small. Speciﬁcally, a 1% increase in revenues corresponds to a 0.135% increase in variable lease expense (compared to 0.124% and 0.122% for operating and ﬁnance lease expenses). For the average ﬁrm in our sample, with $6 billion in revenue and $32 million in variable lease expenses (Table 1), a 1% increase in revenue (or $60 million) is associated with an increase in variable lease expense of $43,200. ## 2 Literature, background, and research question

### 2.1 Literature

Our study contributes to the extensive literature on lease accounting. One important strand examines how incentives shape ﬁrms’ lease-versus-buy decisions (e.g., Beatty et al. 2010; Caskey and Ozel 2019; Eisfeldt and Rampini 2009; Sharpe and Nguyen 1995). Caskey and Ozel (2019) identiﬁes both nonreporting incentives, such as access to ﬁnancing and tax beneﬁts, and reporting incentives, such as window dressing and performance management, as potential motivations for operating leases. While they ﬁnd that ﬁnancing, tax, and operational considerations drive lease decisions, they only ﬁnd weak evidence that reporting incentives matter. Similarly, Beatty et al. (2010) show that liquidity-constrained ﬁrms with low accounting quality are more likely to lease their assets. Another important stream examines two related questions: how companies structure their leases and how capital markets respond to recognized versus disclosed lease amounts. For example, Imhoff and Thomas (1988) show that ﬁrms responded to a previous change in the lease accounting standard—a requirement that ﬁrms recognize ﬁnance leases on their balance sheets—by strategically replacing ﬁnance leases with operating leases, which remained off balance sheet. As described by Bratten et al. (2013), the central question in this literature is whether capital market participants use recognized and disclosed information in the same way. Studies ﬁnd mixed evidence (e.g., Altamuro et al. 2014; Callahan et al. 2013; Ely 1995). For instance, while Callahan et al. (2013) ﬁnd that capital markets price recognized and disclosed leases differently, Bratten et al. (2013) ﬁnd that, when the operating lease disclosures are reliable, capital markets process (unrecognized) operating leases the same way as (recognized) ﬁnance leases. Schipper (2007) suggests that users of ﬁnancial reports often underweight or ignore disclosed information and that the mixed prior evidence stems in part from differences in ﬁnancial-statement users’ characteristics affecting the processing of disclosed and recognized items. This body of work typically examines these questions in the context of the prior lease accounting standards (e.g., Bratten et al. 2013; Imhoff and Thomas 1988). One exception is the work of Yoon (2021), who examines these decisions following the adoption of ASC 842. Yoon (2021) ﬁnds that ﬁrms reduced operating lease commitments after the standard’s adoption, suggesting a strategic shift toward short-term and variable leases. Similarly, Ma and Thomas (2023) document that ﬁrms reduce their operating lease commitments after the adoption of ASC 842 but argue that ﬁrms shift to short-term operating leases, which remain off balance sheet. Our study builds on this literature in three ways. First, we examine the properties of variable lease expenses under ASC 842. Second, we analyze the potential implications of the standard’s differential treatment of variable leases for ﬁrm and investor behavior. Third, we develop a methodology for estimating off-balance-sheet variable lease liabilities and quantify their impact on total debt.

2.2 Accounting for leases under U.S. GAAP

Before the passage of ASC 842, U.S. GAAP addressed lease accounting under ASC 840, which deﬁned a lease as “an agreement conveying the right to use property, plant, or equipment” (ASC 840-10-20). Leases typically involve two parties: the lessee (who obtains the right to use the property) and the lessor (who conveys this right). ASC 840 classiﬁed leases as either capital (later renamed ﬁnance leases under ASC 842) or operating leases. Under ASC 840, capital leases were recognized on the lessee’s balance sheet because such leases shifted all or most of the property’s beneﬁts and risks from the lessor to the lessee (ASC 840-10-10-1). All other leases were classiﬁed as operating leases and remained off balance sheet.8

ThedifferentialtreatmentofleasesunderASC840raisedconcernsamonginvestors, standard setters, and regulators, who worried that ﬁrms were strategically structuring lease arrangements “to meet various accounting, tax, and other goals” (Securities and Exchange Commission 2005). These concerns prompted the FASB to develop a new lease standard beginning in the mid-2000s, culminating in a March 2009 discussion paper that ﬁrst proposed the idea of recording operating leases on the balance sheet (FASB 2016). Building on the feedback from the discussion paper, the FASB’s August 2010 exposure draft mandated balance-sheet recognition for operating leases (IASB/FASB 2010). The draft also addressed variable leases, arguing they met the deﬁnition of a liability for the lessee and an asset for the lessor, and proposed a probability-weighted approach to estimate future variable payments (IASB/FASB 2010). Additionally, lessees would need to reassess their variable lease liabilities in the event of circumstances that could affect future variable payments (FASB 2016). The FASB received feedback from preparers and users who objected to the proposal to record variable leases on the balance sheet (FASB 2016). Preparers argued the proposed approach would be very costly to apply, especially for longer-term leases with payments linked to the lessee’s performance or use of the underlying asset (for example, a 25-year retail-store lease), because it is very difﬁcult to predict the future performance associated with the leased asset. Preparers also pointed out that lessees often entered into leases with variable lease payments because they wanted to share with the lessor the risks of uncertainty about the economic beneﬁts to be derived from the leased asset (FASB 2016). As a result, preparers argued that it would often be difﬁcult to estimate variable lease payments reliably and therefore variable leases were irrelevant to the measurement of lease assets and liabilities. However, some FASB board members countered that variable lease payments are often “in-substance” ﬁxed payments and that excluding them from the measurement of lease assets and liabilities couldcreateincentivesforﬁrmstostructureleasesasvariable(Alqamoussietal.2014). ### 2.3 Research questions

The new lease accounting standard ASC 842 allows ﬁrms to keep variable leases off balance sheet in part because variable leases are presumed to exhibit very different properties—less persistent, less predictable, and more variable—than operating and ﬁnance leases. Our ﬁrst set of analyses empirically tests these assumptions. The answers to these research questions are unclear. On the one hand, we expect variable leases to be, by deﬁnition, more sensitive to changes in ﬁrms’ economic activities. As such, variable lease expenses should exhibit greater variability, lower persistence, and lower predictability than operating or ﬁnance lease expenses. On the other hand, variable lease expenses might exhibit properties similar to other lease types. For example, in its 2010 exposure draft, the FASB argued that lessors and lessees negotiate leases with contingent rental arrangements with a shared understanding of thelikelypayments.Similarly,somepractitionersarguedthatlesseesandlessorswould likely be unwilling to enter into contracts involving large and unpredictable changes in rental payments. Other observers also questioned whether corporate preparers sought to shape the new lease standard to keep a portion of leases off balance sheet. A growing literature shows that parties with a stake in accounting standard setting regularly aim to shape standards to their beneﬁt (e.g., Allen and Ramanna 2013; Gipper et al. 2013; Puro 1984). In the context of ASC 842, Comiran (2014) identiﬁes several motives for ﬁrms to inﬂuence the new standard, such as possible increases in their cost of capital and implementation costs. Standard setters conﬁrmed that ASC 842 was subject to industry lobbying. In his farewell speech, the chairman of the IASB, which developed the standard in close cooperation with the FASB, described the ﬁerce lobbying at the IASB during its development of the new lease accounting standard (Hoogervorst 2021). Some standard setters worried that excluding variable lease payments from the measurement of lease assets and liabilities could create structuring opportunities and incentives (Alqamoussi et al. 2014). Consistent with this concern, studies (Ma and Thomas 2023; Yoon 2021) and anecdotes suggest that ﬁrms restructure their operating leases. For example, Delta reported only $6.8 billion in operating lease liabilities after adopting ASC 842, well below the $11.2 billion expected based on reported operating lease commitments prior to adoption (Eaglesham 2019). Keeping variable lease payments off balance sheet could also affect ﬁrms’ equity betas and credit ratings. For example, in the case of Delta, Moody’s, which had considered Delta’s off-balancesheet operating leases when calculating its total liabilities, used Delta’s substantially

### 4.4 Discussion

While our ﬁrst set of analyses in Sections 4.2 and 4.3 ﬁnds that variable lease expenses are somewhat more sensitive to changes in economic conditions than operating or ﬁnance lease expenses, they show that the persistence and predictability of variable lease expenses resemble those of operating and ﬁnance lease expenses. Taken together, these results suggest that the drivers of variable lease expenses could be generally quite persistent and predictable. While variable leases are designed to respond to changes in the economic driver (ψ > 0), their expenses can remain persistent and predictable if the underlying drivers themselves exhibit high persistence and low variability. Our ﬁndings—that variable, operating, and ﬁnance lease expenses are similarly persistent and predictable—are thus consistent with the idea that the economic drivers of variable lease expenses are highly persistent. As an approximation, we conﬁrm that revenues are highly persistent: a cross-sectional regression of revenues on its lag produces a slope coefﬁcient of 1.05, signiﬁcant at the 1% level. Another complementary explanation for the persistence and predictability of variable lease expenses comes from variable lease payment caps. As discussed in Section 2.2, in a hand-collected sample of 91 lease contracts, approximately 9% of them have a payment ceiling, which constrains payment variability. Our analysis is limited (by data availability) to the properties of one-year-ahead variable lease expenses. The main objection to recognizing variable lease liabilities focused on the difﬁculty of and lack of precision in forecasting variable lease costs over longer horizons. While we cannot speak to longer horizon properties, we argue that short horizon properties of variable lease expenses are most important for measuring lease liabilities. The precision of short horizon forecasts matters more than long horizon ones for measuring lease liabilities because of discounting. Put differently, the impact of forecast errors on the present value of future lease payments declines with the horizon of the forecast. ### 5.1 Lease restructuring

We begin by testing whether ﬁrms restructure part of their operating leases into variable leases after adopting ASC 842. Standard setters worried that companies could change lease terms to keep leases off balance sheet after ASC 842 (Alqamoussi et al. 2014). ### 5.3 Estimating variable lease liabilities

Our previous analyses suggest that market participants do not appear to factor in potential liabilities stemming from variable leases, consistent with anecdotal evidence (Eaglesham 2019). Therefore, we propose a methodology for calculating conservative estimates of off-balance-sheet liabilities associated with variable leases. Our ﬁndings in Table 2 and 4 suggest that variable lease expenses exhibit characteristics that resemble operating lease expenses, implying that liabilities associated with variable lease expenses could be estimated just as reliably as operating lease liabilities. For example, if variable lease expenses largely co-vary with operating lease expenses and if the liabilities could be reliably estimated, we could use the ratio of variable lease expenses to operating lease expenses to estimate the amount of off-balance-sheet variable lease liabilities for a ﬁrm.29

Supplementary analyses corroborate the notion that operating lease expenses provide a useful anchor for variable lease expenses. We ﬁnd that variable lease expenses are approximately 3.5 times as responsive to operating lease expenses as to revenues. Speciﬁcally, a 1% increase in operating lease expenses is associated with a 0.47% increase in variable lease expenses, whereas a 1% increase in revenue leads to a 0.135% increase in variable lease expenses.

29 In principle, similar arguments could be made for ﬁnance lease expenses. However, we use operating lease expenses as an anchor for variable lease expenses because there are twice as many observations of operating lease expense disclosures as there are of ﬁnance lease expense disclosures in our sample.

## 6 Conclusion

ASC 842 requires ﬁrms to recognize both ﬁnance and operating leases on the balance sheet. However, the FASB exempted leases with variable payments, which can be kept off ﬁrms’ balance sheets. The FASB attributed this decision in part based on feedback from preparers about the difﬁculty of reliably estimating future variable lease payments, which can vary due to changes in economic activity associated with the leased asset. This study shows that variable lease expenses exhibit statistical properties resembling those of operating and ﬁnance leases. Like operating and ﬁnance lease expenses, variable lease expenses are highly persistent and predictable. We also ﬁnd that ﬁrms reduce their minimum operating lease commitments and increase their short-term as well as variable lease expenses after adopting ASC 842, potentially because they restructure operating leases as variable leases. After adopting ASC 842, equity betas and credit ratings do not reﬂect potential variable lease liabilities. Conservative estimates show that recognition of variable lease liabilities would increase total debt by 7.1% for the average ﬁrm with variable leases. Overall, our ﬁndings provide evidence on the properties of variable leases and the potential consequences of keeping them off balance sheet.
